label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
**Thursdays with the tea trolley**

When I retired after 41 years of keeping the books for a builders' merchant in Dereham, I assumed I would fill my days easily. I didn't. For about eighteen months I drifted. Most weeks there was no particular reason to put my shoes on and go out, and I got steadily worse at it. In March 2022 I started on the tea trolley in the day therapy unit here at Wensum Vale, and Thursdays fixed that.

I'm writing because the Thursday rota is meant to have six of us on it and at the moment there are four. Two left over the summer, one to Sheffield to be near her grandchildren and one for a knee operation, and neither can be blamed. We are managing, but it would be good to have a couple more people.

I know what many of you think, because I thought it too. Volunteering at a hospice must be either harrowing or terribly skilled, and you must be either a saint or a nurse. I am neither. You need to be able to push a trolley, remember who takes what, and listen. That's all. Forty-one years of making sure the ledgers balanced turns out to be good training for remembering that Margaret has her tea weak with the milk in first.

The day unit sees fourteen to eighteen people on a Thursday. Many come for the art group or the hand massage, or simply for company, and most go home afterwards. It is not a sad place on a Thursday, mostly. It is noisy and rather jolly. Mr Hollis, a retired signalman, takes two sugars and tells me about the 1953 floods every week, slightly differently each time. I have stopped correcting the dates. The bourbons always go first, so we now hide a packet for the late group.

My first week, I spilled a whole jug of milk over the trolley. A patient called Pat laughed so much she had to be given a tissue, and she told me it was the best afternoon she'd had in a month. I'd like to say I planned it, but I didn't. The point is that nobody expects you to be polished. They expect you to turn up and be friendly.

I won't pretend every week is easy. Some days are hard, and when that happens the staff look after us as well as the patients. You are never left on your own with it. That is about all I want to say on the matter, except that I would not swap the good Thursdays for anything.

Here is what it involves:

- **One Thursday a fortnight**, 1.30 to 4pm, in the day therapy unit.
- **A short induction** with Bridget, our volunteer coordinator, which takes about two hours.
- **A brief online food hygiene course**, which the hospice pays for.

That's the lot. No experience needed.

If you are curious but not sure, come to the **volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room**. There will be tea and biscuits (I can't promise bourbons) and no obligation whatsoever. You can look around, ask Bridget anything you like, and go home again if it isn't for you. If you can't make it, ring Bridget on the volunteering line and she will be glad to talk it through.

If you have ever thought "I'd quite like to, but I'm not sure I'd be any good," then you are very probably the sort of person we are looking for. And if you know someone else who might like it, bring them along. Two of you would be even better.

I hope to see you in the Willow Room.

---

I haven't invented a phone number, so you'll want to put Bridget's line in, or link to it. Also check that Bridget and the hospice are happy with Mr Hollis and Pat being mentioned, even by first name or title only. If not, "one of our regulars" will do just as well.
